definition: The practice of multiple individuals or teams working together to achieve shared goals, often facilitated by digital tools.
extendedDefinition: Collaboration is the practice of individuals and teams working together toward shared goals, and in software terms it describes both the work itself and the tools that support it. Effective collaboration combines communication, shared context, and coordinated tasks, which is why collaboration tools span chat, video, documents, and project management. The biggest risk in collaboration software is fragmentation: when discussions, files, and tasks live in separate systems, information goes missing and handoffs break down. Buyers should evaluate collaboration tools on how well they unite content and conversation, how searchable history is, and how smoothly they span contractors, partners, and external stakeholders. Adoption is the other decisive factor: collaboration tools create value only when everyone actually uses them, so ease of use and default behaviors carry unusual weight. Teams should test real cross-functional workflows during trials, including asynchronous handoffs, rather than judging tools on feature lists.
examples: A product team assigns an owner and due date to each decision so work does not disappear into chat messages.
Two departments co-edit a document and verify how comments, version history and access permissions work.
A buyer tests how a contractor can contribute to a project without receiving access to unrelated client records.
description: Collaboration in software teams: shared work, communication, task ownership, version history and decisions that remain accessible.
